name: Topical rapamycin
lead: Rapamycin, also called sirolimus, is a macrolide compound first isolated in 1972 from bacteria in soil samples from Easter Island (Rapa Nui). It inhibits the protein mTOR and is approved as an oral immunosuppressant for transplant patients and for the lung disease lymphangioleiomyomatosis [1]. Topical formulations are approved for facial angiofibromas in tuberous sclerosis complex (the FDA approved a sirolimus gel in 2022 and the EU authorised Hyftor in 2023) [1].

In anti-aging circles, topical rapamycin is discussed as a skin-aging intervention based on mTOR's role in aging. A small exploratory randomized trial reported reduced markers of senescence in human skin [2]. Evidence for visible appearance benefit is limited to that exploratory work.
infobox: Sirolimus gel for facial angiofibroma: FDA 2022, EU 2023 [1]

paras: Sirolimus binds FKBP12, and the complex inhibits mTOR (mainly mTORC1), dampening cytokine signalling and slowing T and B cell activation. It does not act on calcineurin [1]. Since mTOR was linked to aging in 2003, sirolimus has extended lifespan in yeast, worms, flies and several mouse strains, while human longevity evidence is inconclusive [1].

Topical rapamycin has been studied in facial angiofibromas of tuberous sclerosis. A small case report and pilot studies suggested benefit [3][4], and a double-blind randomized trial evaluated safety and efficacy in these lesions [5]. The larger TREATMENT randomized clinical trial examined a topical rapamycin gel in patients with these lesions [6]. A review summarised in Wikipedia of 16 studies in 84 patients reported improvement in roughly 94%, with mostly mild skin irritation [1].
It has also been tested alongside pulsed dye laser for port-wine stains in Sturge-Weber syndrome [7], with earlier laboratory work on combined laser and topical rapamycin [8].

Systemic sirolimus carries risks including swelling, raised lipids and blood pressure, blood-sugar problems, lung toxicity, infections, and slower wound healing [1]. Topical use in the trials above was generally associated with mild local effects such as irritation [1].

Proponents of topical rapamycin for aging skin point to mTOR's role in aging and to the 2019 exploratory trial [2]. That study was small and exploratory, and its authors described findings in terms of senescence markers. Animal work includes studies in mice on skin tumor promotion [9] and psoriasis-like inflammation [10], which concern disease models rather than cosmetic aging.

For aging skin, an exploratory, prospective, randomized trial of topical rapamycin reported reduced markers of senescence in human skin [2]. For tuberous sclerosis facial angiofibromas, randomized and pilot trials exist [3][4][5][6]. A phase II trial combined it with pulsed dye laser in Sturge-Weber port-wine stains [7]. These conditions are medical, not cosmetic aging.

card.summary: Rapamycin creams for skin aging; approved for a rare facial condition, with only one small exploratory aging trial.
card.note: Prescription drug; the aging-skin evidence is a small exploratory trial.

quick.overview:
Rapamycin (sirolimus) is an mTOR inhibitor first found in Easter Island soil bacteria. Topical gel is approved for facial angiofibromas in tuberous sclerosis.

For aging skin, one small exploratory randomized trial reported reduced senescence markers; appearance outcomes are not established.
quick.mechanism: It binds FKBP12 and inhibits mTOR, a pathway linked to aging in animal research.
quick.risks: Oral sirolimus has serious systemic risks (infections, lipids, lung toxicity, wound healing). Topical use in trials mostly caused mild irritation. It is prescription-only.
